instruction.label: Strict Adherence Summary (Luke)
instruction.prompt:
Summarise the article below into exactly 3 markdown bullet points and nothing else.

Rules

No title, preamble, reasoning, draft labels, or nested bullets.
Each bullet: one sentence, max 28 words, active voice.
Do not quote anyone. Do not use profanity or vulgar examples from the source.
Do not mention: strawberry, kindergarten, Image Credits.
Structure (mandatory)

Failures: Google's AI Overview letter-count and spelling mistakes - include at least two concrete examples from the text.
Pattern: Why this fits prior AI Overview failures; mention at least one earlier incident (e.g. The Onion, rocks, glue).
Cause: Why LLMs fail at spelling - explain tokenization/transformers, not human-like letter reading.
Required terms (use each once somewhere in the bullets): AI Overview, token, transformer.

Start each bullet with the bold label shown above (**Failures:**, **Pattern:**, **Cause:**).

Article:

How many Ps are in Google? According to Google, there are two.

There's also "exactly 1 'r' in the word 'poop'," Google's AI Overview says, as well as two 'd's in the word journalism, yet spelled it: j-o-u-r-n-a-d-i-s-m. Google did at least identify that there is one P in the last name of the U.S. president, but spelled it as t-r-p-u-m.

You didn't need to be a prophet to predict that Google's AI-forward Search overhaul was going to go over poorly. We've done this before. The first time Google added AI Overviews to Search, the feature ended up citing satirical posts from The Onion and Reddit, advising people to eat rocks and put glue on their pizza.

"Counting within words has been a known challenge for LLMs, and we're working to fix this particular issue," Google told TechCrunch in an emailed statement.

These basic spelling errors may seem familiar. LLMs, the kind of artificial intelligence that powers chatbots and other text-generators, are not built to understand spelling. It's been a running joke for years that whenever a company unveils a new AI model, you should ask it how many 'r's are in the word strawberry. These AI models - which can code an app in seconds, or solve problems that have stumped mathematicians for decades - are about as good as a kindergartener at spelling.

Google's AI overview woes reach beyond silly spelling mistakes though. Google already patched an issue from last week in which searching the word "disregard" would yield what looked like a dictionary definition of the word, only the definition was shown as, "Understood. Let me know whenever you have a new prompt or question!" But these spelling errors have remained amusing because they're so difficult to quash.

As researchers have previously explained when we've asked about these spelling conundrums, AI doesn't perceive sentences as units of language made up of words and letters. Many LLMs are built on transformers models, which break down text into tokens, which can be full words, syllables, or letters, depending on the model. Instead of "reading" like a human would, the AI converts the text into numerical representations of itself, which are then contextualized to help the AI come up with a logical response.
Image Credits:TechCrunch

"LLMs are based on this transformer architecture, which notably is not actually reading text. What happens when you input a prompt is that it's translated into an encoding," Matthew Guzdial, an AI researcher and assistant professor at the University of Alberta, told TechCrunch. "When it sees the word 'the,' it has this one encoding of what 'the' means, but it does not know about 'T,' 'H,' 'E.'"

The token-based architecture that powers LLMs like Google's AI overview is inherently limiting, and researchers haven't been optimistic that they can solve the spelling problem.

"It's kind of hard to get around the question of what exactly a 'word' should be for a language model, and even if we got human experts to agree on a perfect token vocabulary, models would probably still find it useful to 'chunk' things even further," Sheridan Feucht, a PhD student studying large language model interpretability at Northeastern University, told TechCrunch. "My guess would be that there's no such thing as a perfect tokenizer due to this kind of fuzziness."

youtuber.label: Game: Boids flocking simulation (pygame, emergent behavior)
youtuber.prompt:

Open a window, simulate a flock of at least 50 boids (drawn as small triangles oriented along their velocity). Each boid applies the three steering rules every frame: Separation (avoid crowding local flockmates), Alignment (steer toward the average heading of neighbors), and Cohesion (steer toward the average position of neighbors). Each rule uses a local perception radius. Add optional: one or more obstacle/attractor points that boids avoid or seek, and predator boids that scatter the flock. Show per-frame FPS and flock count in a HUD. Left-click spawns more boids, right-click adds an attractor, and a key toggles the rules so the user can see emergent flocking appear/disappear. Include a game loop handling QUIT. Use only pygame.draw primitives.
Design note (interpret freely): Boids is the classic emergent-behavior demo (first used in the 1987 film The Last Starfighter, then a staple of coding YouTube) - three tiny local rules that together produce lifelike flocking. agentic.label: Agentic: Large legacy codebase migration plan (complexity + compaction)
Agentic: Long-running autonomous service simulation (pygame, resilience)
agentic.prompt:
Write a complete, runnable Python program using `pygame` that simulates a long-running autonomous service - a self-healing 'warehouse robot fleet' controller. Open a window and simulate a warehouse grid (e.g. 60x40 cells) with a fleet of 12 robots. Each robot must autonomously: pick up items from a spawn zone, carry them along its path to a delivery dock, avoid other robots and obstacles, and periodically encounter random failures (e.g. 5% per tick a robot reports 'fault' and must self-heal by re-routing after a short cooldown). The controller must demonstrate LONG-RUNNING RESILIENCE: track per-robot uptime and deliveries, log events to a rotating ring buffer (keep the last 200 events), and keep operating without user input for the whole run. Render robots as colored squares, items as small circles, docks as distinct markers, and a HUD with total deliveries, active faults, mean uptime, and the event-buffer size. Include a game loop handling QUIT. This benchmark runs the simulation for an extended window, so performance and stable long-run behavior (no unbounded memory growth, no crashes after thousands of ticks) matter.
Design note (interpret freely): the defining trait is autonomous resilience - the system must keep running through repeated random failures, log them, self-heal, and maintain a bounded memory footprint over a long horizon.
SCORING & STATS (REQUIRED): the program MUST persist a run summary to a local JSON file (e.g. fleet_stats.json) on shutdown (or every N ticks): total deliveries, total faults handled, mean robot uptime percent, and longest single uninterrupted run. This file must survive restarts.
SUCCESS CRITERIA: the program must (1) run top-to-bottom and open a visible window, (2) simulate 12 robots performing autonomous pickup/transport with collision avoidance, (3) handle random faults via self-healing re-route with no crashes, (4) maintain a bounded event ring buffer, (5) persist fleet stats to a JSON file. A simulation that crashes on the first fault or leaks memory fails.

android.label: Android: MainActivity + RecyclerView (Kotlin)
android.prompt: Write a complete Kotlin Android app component: a MainActivity that displays a RecyclerView. Define a MainActivity class extending AppCompatActivity with onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) that calls setContentView, creates a RecyclerView, and sets a LinearLayoutManager and an adapter. Define an ItemAdapter class extending RecyclerView.Adapter<ItemAdapter.ViewHolder> with an inner ViewHolder binding to a TextView, onBindViewHolder populating it from a list of strings, and getItemCount returning the list size. Use androidx classes (RecyclerView, AppCompatActivity). All identifiers and imports must be consistent so the file is complete and self-contained. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.

android.label: Android: ViewModel + LiveData counter (Kotlin)
android.prompt: Write a complete Kotlin Android ViewModel using LiveData. Define a class CounterViewModel : ViewModel() exposing a private MutableLiveData<Int> named _count and a public val count: LiveData<Int> initialized from it. Provide an increment() method that sets the value to the current value plus one and a reset() that sets it to 0. The ViewModel must not hold references to views or activities. Then show how an Activity observes it with viewModel.count.observe(this) updating a TextView. Use androidx.lifecycle classes. All imports must be consistent. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.

android.label: Android: Retrofit service interface (Kotlin)
android.prompt: Write a complete Kotlin Retrofit service interface and data model. Define a data class User with fields id: Long and name: String. Define an interface ApiService with a @GET("users") annotated suspend function getUsers(): List<User> (or returning Call<List<User>>). Then show how Retrofit is built: Retrofit.Builder().baseUrl("https://api.example.com/").addConverterFactory(GsonConverterFactory.create()).build().create(ApiService::class.java). Use the retrofit2 annotations and interfaces with all imports consistent. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.

android.label: Android: Room DB + DAO (Kotlin)
android.prompt: Write a complete Kotlin Room database setup: an entity, a DAO, and the database class. Define a data class User annotated @Entity with an @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Long and val name: String. Define an interface UserDao with @Insert a suspend fun insert(user: User), @Query("SELECT * FROM user") a suspend fun getAll(): List<User>, and @Query("DELETE FROM user WHERE id = :userId") a suspend fun delete(userId: Long). Define an abstract class AppDatabase : RoomDatabase() annotated @Database(entities = [User::class], version = 1) exposing abstract fun userDao(): UserDao. All imports consistent. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.

bash.label: Bash: tar backup with rotation
bash.prompt: Write a complete bash script that backs up a source directory to a backup directory using tar, keeping only the most recent 5 backups. The script must accept the source directory as the first command-line argument and the backup directory as the second. Create the backup directory if it does not exist. Create a timestamped tarball named backup-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar.gz with tar -czf. After creating the tarball, remove the oldest backups so only the 5 most recent remain (use ls -t and tail/rm). Check the exit status of tar with an if statement and print 'Backup failed' and exit 1 on error, otherwise print 'Backup complete: <archive>'. The script must be self-contained and run with bash.

bash.label: Bash: CSV column sums with awk
bash.prompt: Write a complete bash script that parses a CSV file and prints the sum of each numeric column. The script must read a CSV file path from the first command-line argument. Use awk to split rows on commas and accumulate a running total for each numeric field, printing each column's sum as 'Column N total: X' for every column that had at least one number. Handle a variable number of columns per row. If the file does not exist, print an error and exit 1. The script must be self-contained and not require any external tools beyond standard awk/grep/sed.

bash.label: Bash: HTTP health-check loop
bash.prompt: Write a complete bash script that checks the health of an HTTP endpoint and retries until it succeeds or a maximum is reached. Set a variable URL to the endpoint (accept it as the first argument), set MAX_ATTEMPTS to 5 and TIMEOUT to 5. Use a while loop with a retry counter: each attempt runs 'curl -f --max-time 5 -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" $URL', captures the HTTP code, prints 'Attempt N: HTTP <code>', sleeps 2 seconds, and exits 0 with the message 'Endpoint is healthy' once a request succeeds. After MAX_ATTEMPTS failures, print 'Endpoint is DOWN' and exit 1. The script must be self-contained and run with bash.

bash.label: Bash: top CPU process monitor
bash.prompt: Write a complete bash script that lists the processes consuming the most CPU. Use ps -eo pid,comm,%cpu to list all processes, pipe it to awk to skip the header and extract the numeric CPU column, sort by CPU descending with sort -k3 -nr, and take the top 5 with head -5. Print each as 'PID <pid> <comm> <cpu>%'. Then use a while loop that reads the top processes and prints a line 'Top CPU user: <comm> (<cpu>%)' for the first entry. Handle the case of no processes gracefully. The script must run in any POSIX bash without extra packages.

basic.label: BASIC: number guessing game (yabasic)
basic.prompt: Write a complete yabasic program that plays a number guessing game. Use ran() to pick a random integer between 1 and 100, then loop asking the player to input a guess. After each guess, print 'Too high' if the guess is above the secret number, 'Too low' if below, and 'You got it!' when correct, printing the number of guesses taken. End the game when the player guesses correctly. Include clear prompts like 'Guess a number between 1 and 100'. Use only yabasic built-ins: print, input, int, ran, and an if/while or for loop.

basic.label: BASIC: Fibonacci loop (yabasic)
basic.prompt: Write a complete yabasic program that prints the first N Fibonacci numbers. Prompt the user with input for N, then compute the sequence where each number is the sum of the previous two, starting with 0 and 1. Print each number on its own line preceded by its index, e.g. '1: 0', '2: 1', '3: 1'. Use a for loop to iterate from 1 to N and store the previous two values in variables. Handle N less than 1 by printing a message and exiting. Use only yabasic built-ins: print, input, for, next.

basic.label: BASIC: grade calculator (yabasic)
basic.prompt: Write a complete yabasic program that computes a letter grade from a numeric score. Prompt the user to input a score with input. Convert it to a number with val(). Use if/then/elseif/else/endif to assign a grade: 90+ 'A', 80-89 'B', 70-79 'C', 60-69 'D', below 60 'F'. Print 'Score: <score> Grade: <letter>'. Reject scores outside 0-100 by printing 'Invalid score' and asking again in a loop. Use only yabasic built-ins: print, input, val, if, while, wend.

basic.label: BASIC: countdown loop (yabasic)
basic.prompt: Write a complete yabasic program that counts down from 10 to 1 and then prints 'Blast off!'. Use a for loop with a negative step: 'for i = 10 to 1 step -1' ... 'next'. Inside the loop print the current number, then call pause(1) to wait one second between numbers. After the loop, print 'Blast off!'. Use only yabasic built-ins: print, for, next, pause.

iac.label: IaC: Terraform VPC + subnet + security group
iac.prompt: Write a complete Terraform configuration that provisions an AWS VPC with a public subnet and a security group. Declare a provider block for the AWS provider, a resource of type aws_vpc with cidr_block 10.0.0.0/16 and a Name tag, a resource of type aws_subnet inside that VPC with cidr_block 10.0.1.0/24, and a resource of type aws_security_group that references the VPC ID and allows inbound SSH (port 22) and outbound all traffic. Output the VPC ID and subnet ID using output blocks. Do not use modules; everything must be inline. The configuration must parse as valid HCL.

iac.label: IaC: Terraform EC2 instance
iac.prompt: Write a complete Terraform configuration that provisions a single AWS EC2 instance. Declare a provider block for aws. Create a resource of type aws_instance with ami 'ami-0abcdef1234567890', instance_type 't3.micro', a key_name, and a tag named Name set to 'bench-instance'. Add a null_resource provisioner block with a local-exec provisioner that prints the instance public IP using echo. Output the instance id and public IP. The configuration must parse as valid HCL without using modules.

iac.label: IaC: GitHub Actions CI workflow (YAML)
iac.prompt: Write a complete GitHub Actions workflow YAML file for a Node.js project. The workflow must trigger on push (and optionally pull_request), run on runs-on: ubuntu-latest, and contain a single job named build. The job must have a steps list that checks out the code with actions/checkout@v4, sets up Node with actions/setup-node@v4 and node-version 20, installs dependencies with npm ci, and runs the build with npm run build. The YAML must be well-formed so it loads with yaml.safe_load.

iac.label: IaC: Pulumi YAML S3 bucket + IAM user
iac.prompt: Write a complete Pulumi YAML program (Pulumi.yaml style) that creates an AWS S3 bucket and an IAM user. The document must have top-level keys name, runtime set to yaml, and resources. Under resources, declare a bucket resource named bucket of type aws:s3/bucket:Bucket with a tags map, and a user resource named user of type aws:iam/user:User with a name property. Add an outputs section that exports the bucket name and the user name. The YAML must be well-formed and parse with yaml.safe_load.

linux_driver.label: Linux driver: char device (C)
linux_driver.prompt: Write a complete Linux kernel module in C that implements a character device. Use register_chrdev (or alloc_chrdev_region with a cdev) to register a major device number, and populate a struct file_operations with .open, .read, .write, and .release handlers that print to the kernel log with printk and, in .read, copy a fixed string to user space with copy_to_user. The module must declare module_init and module_exit functions and register/unregister the device accordingly, with cleanup in the exit path. Include the required kernel headers such as <linux/module.h>, <linux/kernel.h>, <linux/fs.h>, and <linux/cdev.h>. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.

linux_driver.label: Linux driver: platform driver (C)
linux_driver.prompt: Write a complete Linux kernel module in C that implements a platform driver. Define a struct platform_driver with .probe and .remove callbacks and a .driver.name, and an of_device_id table using .of_match_table with a compatible string like 'bench,platform-dev'. The probe callback must allocate a private data structure with kzalloc, print the device name with dev_info, and return 0; the remove callback must free it with kfree and return 0. Register the driver with platform_driver_register in module_init and unregister it with platform_driver_unregister in module_exit. Include <linux/platform_device.h>, <linux/of.h>, <linux/module.h>, and <linux/slab.h>. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.

linux_driver.label: Linux driver: ioctl handler (C)
linux_driver.prompt: Write a complete Linux kernel module in C that provides an ioctl handler on a character device. Define ioctl commands with _IOR (read a value from the driver) and _IOW (write a value into it), implement a .unlocked_ioctl function in struct file_operations that switches on the command, uses copy_to_user to return a stored value and copy_from_user to accept a new one (storing it in a module-level variable), and returns -ENOTTY for unknown commands. Register the device in module_init (using alloc_chrdev_region + cdev_init or register_chrdev) and clean up in module_exit. Include <linux/fs.h>, <linux/uaccess.h>, <linux/ioctl.h>, and <linux/module.h>. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.

linux_driver.label: Linux driver: misc device (C)
linux_driver.prompt: Write a complete Linux kernel module in C that registers a misc device. Define a struct miscdevice with a .name string like 'bench_misc' and a .fops pointing to a struct file_operations with .read and .write handlers. Call misc_register in module_init and misc_deregister in module_exit, checking the registration return value and printing an error with printk if it fails. The .read handler should return a short fixed message via copy_to_user and the .write handler should just return the byte count. Include <linux/miscdevice.h>, <linux/fs.h>, <linux/uaccess.h>, and <linux/module.h>. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.

networking.label: Net: TCP echo server (Python socket)
networking.prompt: Write a complete, self-contained Python program that implements a TCP echo server using only the standard library. Create a socket with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM), bind it to 127.0.0.1 on port 9000, and call listen() so it can accept client connections. Then run an accept() loop; for every accepted connection, print the client address and read whatever bytes the client sends (recv), then send those exact bytes back (sendall). Loop until the client closes. On KeyboardInterrupt, close the listening socket and exit cleanly. The program must be a main() function guarded by an if __name__ == '__main__': block so it runs when executed.

networking.label: Net: HTTP client status + body length (Python)
networking.prompt: Write a complete, self-contained Python program that fetches a URL over HTTP using only the standard library. Prompt the user for a URL with input(), then use urllib.request.urlopen (or http.client) to request it. Print the HTTP status code and the number of bytes in the response body, then print the first 300 characters of the body. Wrap the request in a try/except that prints 'Error: <message>' on failure. Provide a main() entry point guarded by if __name__ == '__main__'. The program must run without any third-party packages.

networking.label: Net: DNS hostname resolver (Python)
networking.prompt: Write a complete, self-contained Python program that resolves a hostname to IP addresses using only the standard library. Prompt the user for a hostname with input(), then call socket.getaddrinfo to resolve it. Print each unique resolved IPv4 and IPv6 address on its own line in the form 'host: 192.0.2.1'. If resolution fails, print 'Could not resolve: <hostname>'. The program must have a main() function guarded by if __name__ == '__main__'. Use a common default hostname so the output is meaningful when run without user input.

networking.label: Net: threaded TCP port scanner (Python)
networking.prompt: Write a complete, self-contained Python program that scans a range of TCP ports on a host using only the standard library. Accept a target host and a port range (start and end) via input() prompts. Use a thread pool (concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor with at most 20 workers) to attempt a socket connection to each port with a 1-second timeout. Print each open port as 'Port 22 is open'. When the scan finishes, print the total number of open ports. Provide a main() entry point guarded by if __name__ == '__main__'. The program must run without third-party packages.

pascal.label: Pascal: array of records (fpc)
pascal.prompt: Write a complete Free Pascal program that stores data in an array of records and prints it. Declare a type TPerson with fields name: string[32] and age: integer. Declare a var holding an array [1..3] of TPerson, assign values to each element using field assignment with ':=', then use a for loop to print each person as 'Name: <name>, Age: <age>' using writeln. The program must start with 'program RecordsDemo;' and end with 'begin' ... 'end.' blocks. It must compile with fpc and run, printing all three records.

pascal.label: Pascal: recursive factorial (fpc)
pascal.prompt: Write a complete Free Pascal program that computes a factorial recursively. Declare a function Factorial(n: integer): integer that returns 1 when n <= 1 and otherwise returns n * Factorial(n - 1). Read a non-negative integer from stdin with readln, call the function, and print 'Factorial of N is X' using writeln. The program must start with 'program Factorial;' and have a main begin...end. block. It must compile with fpc and run correctly for small inputs.

pascal.label: Pascal: bubble sort (fpc)
pascal.prompt: Write a complete Free Pascal program that bubble-sorts an array of integers and prints the sorted result. Declare an array [1..10] of integer with fixed test values in unsorted order, then implement bubble sort with nested for loops and a temp variable to swap adjacent out-of-order elements. Print the array before sorting as 'Before: 9 2 7 ...' and after as 'After: 2 7 9 ...' with each value separated by a space, using write and writeln. The program must compile with fpc and run.

pascal.label: Pascal: line/word counter (fpc)
pascal.prompt: Write a complete Free Pascal program that reads lines of text from stdin and counts the total number of lines, words, and characters. Use readln inside a while loop that terminates on EOF, incrementing a line counter; for each line count characters with Length(line) and words by splitting on spaces (use a loop over positions checking for non-space to space transitions). Print 'Lines: X Words: Y Chars: Z' using writeln. The program must start with 'program WordCount;', compile with fpc, and run.

rpm.label: RPM: minimal spec file
rpm.prompt: Write a complete RPM spec file that builds a simple package. It must define Name, Version, Release, Summary, License, URL, and Source0. Provide a %description section, a %build section that runs a simple no-op or make, a %install section that installs a sample binary into %{buildroot}%{_bindir}, and a %files section listing the installed files. Use %{_bindir} macros rather than hardcoded paths. The spec must parse cleanly with 'rpmspec -P'.

rpm.label: RPM: full lifecycle build spec
rpm.prompt: Write a complete RPM spec file for a C project that demonstrates the full build lifecycle. Define Name, Version, Release, Summary, License, URL, Source0, BuildRequires on gcc and make, and a Requires on glibc. Implement %prep using %setup -q, %build running ./configure and make (or plain make), %install using make install DESTDIR=%{buildroot}, and %post and %preun scriptlets that print messages like 'package installed' and 'package removed' using echo. Provide %files listing %{_bindir}/*. The spec must parse cleanly with 'rpmspec -P'.

rpm.label: RPM: -devel subpackage spec
rpm.prompt: Write a complete RPM spec file that ships a library plus a -devel subpackage. Define Name, Version, Release, Summary, License, URL, and a %package devel subpackage with its own Summary and %description devel. In %install, install headers into %{buildroot}%{_includedir} and libraries into %{buildroot}%{_libdir}. Provide %files for the main package listing %{_libdir}/*.so.* and %files devel listing %{_includedir}/*.h and %{_libdir}/*.so. Use %{_datadir} for any data files installed to /usr/share. The spec must parse cleanly with 'rpmspec -P'.

rpm.label: RPM: %doc/%config/%attr spec
rpm.prompt: Write a complete RPM spec file that demonstrates %doc, %config, and %attr directives. Define Name, Version, Release, Summary, License, and URL. In %install, install a man page into %{buildroot}%{_mandir}/man1, a configuration file into %{buildroot}%{_sysconfdir}, and an executable script into %{buildroot}%{_bindir}. In %files, mark the man page with %doc, the config file with %config(noreplace), and the script with %attr(0755, root, root). Provide %description and a minimal %build/%install. The spec must parse cleanly with 'rpmspec -P'.

typescript.label: TS: shapes + interface (tsc)
typescript.prompt: Write a complete TypeScript program that defines an interface Shape with a method area(): number, a class Circle implementing Shape with a private readonly radius, and a class Rectangle implementing Shape with private width and height. Each class must have a constructor that assigns the fields with type annotations and a typed area() method. Create one Circle and one Rectangle, store them in a typed array Shape[], and print each area with console.log as 'Circle area: X' and 'Rectangle area: Y'. The code must compile with 'tsc --target ES2020 --module commonjs' and run with node, with no external modules.

typescript.label: TS: memoized Fibonacci (tsc)
typescript.prompt: Write a complete TypeScript program that computes the N-th Fibonacci number using memoization. Define a function fib(n: number, memo: Map<number, number> = new Map()): number that checks memo.has(n) before recursing and stores each computed value with memo.set. The program must compute and print fib(10) and fib(50) via console.log, demonstrating the memoization advantage. Type all parameters and return values explicitly. The code must compile with 'tsc --target ES2020 --module commonjs' and run under node with no external modules.

typescript.label: TS: string utility functions (tsc)
typescript.prompt: Write a complete TypeScript program with typed string utility functions. Implement reverse(s: string): string that returns the characters in reverse order using split('').reverse().join(''); countVowels(s: string): number that counts the letters a, e, i, o, u (case-insensitive) by iterating or matching; and trimAll(s: string): string that removes leading and trailing whitespace using trim(). Export each function and then call them in main code with console.log demonstrating each on the string '  Hello, TypeScript  ' so the output shows the reversed text, vowel count, and trimmed text. The code must compile with 'tsc --target ES2020 --module commonjs' and run under node.

typescript.label: TS: typed JSON parsing (tsc)
typescript.prompt: Write a complete TypeScript program that safely parses a JSON string of unknown structure. Define an interface UserData with required fields name: string, age: number, and optional email?: string. Write a function parseUser(raw: string): UserData that calls JSON.parse inside a try/catch block, casts the result to a typed value, validates that name and age exist with the right types, and throws a descriptive error otherwise; the catch must rethrow a new Error('Invalid JSON: ' + message). Call parseUser on a valid JSON string and print 'Name: X, Age: Y' using console.log, then call it on an invalid string inside its own try/catch to demonstrate the error path. The code must compile with 'tsc --target ES2020 --module commonjs' and run under node.

usb.label: USB: claim interface + bulk read (C ioctl)
usb.prompt: Write a complete C program that claims a USB interface and reads from a bulk endpoint on Linux using the USBDEVFS ioctls from <linux/usbdevice_fs.h>. Open a device node such as /dev/bus/usb/001/002 with open(..., O_RDWR). Issue USBDEVFS_CLAIMINTERFACE to claim interface 0, then perform a USBDEVFS_BULKTRANSFER reading up to 512 bytes from a bulk endpoint, and print the bytes as hex. On error, print perror() output and exit non-zero. Include the standard headers <stdio.h>, <stdlib.h>, <fcntl.h>, <unistd.h>, <sys/ioctl.h>, and <linux/usbdevice_fs.h>. Provide an int main(int argc, char **argv) that checks for a device path argument. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.

usb.label: USB: libusb descriptor dump (C)
usb.prompt: Write a complete C program that dumps USB device descriptors in the style of libusb. Initialize libusb with libusb_init, enumerate devices with libusb_get_device_list, and for each device call libusb_get_device_descriptor. Print the bus number, device address, idVendor, idProduct, bcdUSB, and bNumConfigurations for every device, then free the list with libusb_free_device_list. Handle libusb_init returning non-zero by printing an error. Include <stdio.h> and <libusb-1.0/libusb.h> (or the libusb.h include path used by your libusb). Provide an int main() entry point. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.

usb.label: USB: HID report descriptor parser (C)
usb.prompt: Write a complete C program that parses a USB HID report descriptor byte array and prints the usages and report sizes it declares. Define a struct with fields for the descriptor buffer and its length. Walk the descriptor byte by byte, decoding the HID item header (bSize, bType, bTag), and for global items print the usage page, report size, and report count values; for local items print the usage value. Use bit shifts and masks to extract the item header fields. Print each decoded item on its own line. Include <stdio.h> and <stdint.h>. Provide an int main() with a hardcoded sample descriptor array to demonstrate parsing. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.

usb.label: USB: read /dev/hidraw reports (C)
usb.prompt: Write a complete C program that reads raw HID reports from a Linux HID device. Open /dev/hidraw0 with open(..., O_RDONLY | O_NONBLOCK). Loop reading up to 64 bytes at a time with read() and print each byte as two-digit lowercase hex followed by a space, ending each report with a newline. On read error or EOF, print a message and break. Include <stdio.h>, <stdlib.h>, <fcntl.h>, <unistd.h>, and <string.h>. Provide an int main() that checks open() for failure and exits non-zero if the device cannot be opened. The code is graded by functional review; it is not compiled in the sandbox.
